claim: Macrophages transfer mitochondria to MDA-MB-231 breast cancer cells in vitro.
source: We observed mitochondrial transfer from macrophages to 231 cells using live cell confocal microscopy (Figure 1b, arrowheads) and flow cytometry (Figure 1c–d; flow cytometry scheme in Figure 1—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: Supported by confocal microscopy images and flow cytometry data showing macrophage mitochondria in cancer cells

claim: Mitochondrial transfer from macrophages to cancer cells occurs at a rate of 0.84% across donors.
source: Thus, due to the low rates of mitochondrial transfer across macrophage donors (0.84%, Figure 1d), we subsequently took advantage of single-cell, high-resolution approaches – rather than bulk approaches – to follow the fate and functional status of transferred mitochondria.
evidence: Quantified from flow cytometry data aggregated across 14 donors

claim: Macrophages transfer mitochondria to MDA-MB-468 and A375 cancer cell lines.
source: With these methods, a range of transfer efficiencies were observed, which we attribute to donor-to-donor variability (Figure 1d), yet mitochondrial transfer was consistently observed in 231 cells, as well as to another breast cancer line, MDA-MB-468, and a melanoma cell line, A375 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: Demonstrated by flow cytometry across multiple cancer cell lines

claim: Macrophages exhibit reduced mitochondrial transfer efficiencies to non-malignant MCF10A cells compared to malignant cells.
source: We observed reduced mitochondrial transfer efficiencies to MCF10A cells, with no significant differences compared to control (Figure 1—figure supplement 1c), suggesting that macrophages exhibit higher mitochondrial transfer efficiencies to malignant cells.
evidence: Flow cytometry data comparing transfer rates to malignant versus non-malignant cells

claim: Transferred mitochondria contain the outer mitochondrial membrane protein TOMM20.
source: Transferred mitochondria contain a key outer mitochondrial membrane protein, TOMM20 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1d, arrowhead) and mitochondrial DNA (Figure 1—figure supplement 1e, arrowhead), suggesting that intact organelles are transferred to 231 cells.
evidence: Immunofluorescence imaging showing TOMM20 in transferred mitochondria

claim: Transferred mitochondria contain mitochondrial DNA.
source: Transferred mitochondria contain a key outer mitochondrial membrane protein, TOMM20 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1d, arrowhead) and mitochondrial DNA (Figure 1—figure supplement 1e, arrowhead), suggesting that intact organelles are transferred to 231 cells.
evidence: Microscopy showing DNA staining in transferred mitochondria (83% contain DNA)

claim: Macrophage mitochondrial transfer to cancer cells requires cell-to-cell contact.
source: These data showed that mitochondrial transfer increased dramatically under conditions where 231 cells could contact macrophages directly (Figure 1—figure supplement 1g and h). Taken together, these results suggest that macrophage mitochondrial transfer to cancer cells likely requires cell-to-cell contact.
evidence: Trans-well experiments and conditioned media experiments showing transfer only occurs with direct contact

claim: Cancer cells that receive macrophage mitochondria exhibit significant changes in canonical cell proliferation-related pathways.
source: To determine the effects of macrophage mitochondrial transfer on cancer cells, we performed single cell RNA-sequencing on cancer cells that received macrophage mitochondria. These data revealed that mitochondrial transfer induced significant changes in canonical cell proliferation-related pathways (Figure 1—figure supplement 2a).
evidence: Single-cell RNA-sequencing data analyzed with Ingenuity Pathway Analysis

claim: Cancer cells with macrophage mitochondria show a significant increase in the percentage of cells in G2 and M phases of the cell cycle.
source: To follow up on the RNA-sequencing results, we used flow cytometry to evaluate proliferation changes, and found significant increases in the percent of cells within the G2 and Mitotic (M) phases of the cell cycle in recipient cells, as compared to their co-cultured counterparts that did not receive mitochondria (Figure 1e; Figure 1—figure supplement 2b-d).
evidence: Flow cytometry analysis of Ki-67 and DNA content showing increased G2/M populations

claim: Recipient cancer cells complete cytokinesis at rates equivalent to non-recipient counterparts.
source: These cells were not undergoing cell cycle arrest, as we found that recipient cells completed cytokinesis at rates equivalent to their co-cultured non-recipient counterparts (Figure 1—figure supplement 2e).
evidence: Time-lapse imaging quantifying cytokinesis completion over 48 hours

claim: Cancer cells with macrophage mitochondria exhibit significantly increased specific growth rates compared to cells without transferred mitochondria.
source: Consistent with the flow cytometry-based cell cycle analysis, the specific growth rates increased significantly in 231 cells with macrophage mitochondria compared to 231 cells that did not receive mitochondria (Figure 1f).
evidence: Quantitative phase imaging (QPI) measurements of dry mass over time in 60 control and 115 recipient cells

claim: Daughter cells that inherit macrophage mitochondria exhibit increased growth rates compared to sister cells that do not inherit them.
source: Daughter cells that inherited the 'parent's' macrophage mitochondria exhibited an increase in their rate of change of dry mass over time versus sister cells that did not inherit macrophage mitochondria (Figure 1—figure supplement 3a-c).
evidence: QPI tracking of five parent-daughter cell triads showing differential growth rates

claim: The proliferation phenotype in recipient cancer cells is sustained across cell divisions.
source: These experiments indicate that the proliferation phenotype in recipient cancer cells is sustained.
evidence: Based on daughter cell growth rate measurements and cell cycle analyses

claim: Blocking cells in G1 phase with Palbociclib does not change mitochondrial transfer rates.
source: Thus, to test between these hypotheses, we first blocked cells in the G1-phase of the cell cycle by treating co-cultures with a CDK4/6 inhibitor, Palbociclib (Figure 1—figure supplement 3d), and we observed no changes in mitochondrial transfer rates (Figure 1—figure supplement 3e).
evidence: Flow cytometry data comparing transfer rates with and without Palbociclib treatment

claim: Enhanced proliferation in recipient cells is not due to proliferative cells being more capable of receiving transfer.
source: These data indicate that the enhanced proliferation observed in recipient cells is not due to proliferative cells more readily receiving transfer.
evidence: Based on Palbociclib experiments showing no change in transfer rates when proliferation is blocked

claim: Cancer cells that retain purified macrophage mitochondria exhibit increased percentage of cells in G2/M phase compared to cells that lost the mitochondria.
source: We also found that cancer cells that had retained the macrophage mitochondria exhibited an increased percentage of cells in the G2/M phase of the cell cycle compared to cancer cells that had lost the macrophage mitochondria (Figure 1i-j).
evidence: Flow cytometry analysis 48 hours after FACS-isolation of cells with purified macrophage mitochondria

claim: Macrophage mitochondrial transfer causes cancer cell proliferation rather than being merely correlative.
source: Together with the QPI results, these results support the model that macrophage mitochondrial transfer promotes a sustained pro-growth and proliferative effect in both recipient and subsequent daughter cells.
evidence: Based on purified mitochondria experiments and daughter cell tracking

claim: Transferred macrophage mitochondria remain distinct from the recipient host mitochondrial network and do not fuse with it.
source: We performed time-lapse confocal microscopy on co-cultures and found that in cancer cells with macrophage mitochondria, macrophage-derived mito-mEm+ mitochondria remained distinct from the recipient host mitochondrial network. Cancer cells were cocultured with macrophages for 12 hr and subjected to an additional 15 hr of timelapse microscopy, and we observed no detectable loss of the fluorescent signal at transferred mitochondria throughout the course of imaging (Figure 2a, arrowhead; Video 1). Thus, transferred macrophage mitochondria did not appear to fuse with the existing endogenous mitochondrial network in recipient cells.
evidence: Time-lapse confocal microscopy over 15 hours showing persistent distinct fluorescent signal

claim: All transferred mitochondria lack membrane potential as indicated by absence of MitoTracker Deep Red staining.
source: To our surprise, all of the transferred mitochondria were MTDR-negative (Figure 2b, top left). This was also confirmed using a different mitochondrial membrane potential-sensitive dye, Tetramethylrhodamine Methyl Ester (TMRM; Figure 1—figure supplement 1e). These results suggested that the transferred mitochondria lacked membrane potential.
evidence: Live imaging with MTDR and TMRM dyes showing 100% of transferred mitochondria are negative for membrane potential markers

claim: The majority (57%) of transferred mitochondria do not colocalize with LysoTracker signal, indicating they are not being degraded in lysosomes.
source: To determine whether these membrane potential-deficient transferred mitochondria were subjected to lysosomal degradation, we labeled lysosomes and acidic vesicles with a dye, LysoTracker, and found that the majority of transferred mitochondria (57%) did not co-localize with the LysoTracker signal (Figure 2b, top right).
evidence: Fluorescence microscopy with LysoTracker staining in 24 cells from 4 donors

claim: 91% of transferred mitochondria are not encapsulated by membranous structures.
source: Next, we utilized another dye which stains cellular membranes, MemBrite, and observed that 91% of transferred mitochondria were not encapsulated by a membranous structure, thus also excluding sequestration as a mechanism for explaining the lack of degradation or interaction with the endogenous mitochondrial network (Figure 2—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: MemBrite staining showing lack of membrane encapsulation in 11 cells from 1 donor

claim: Transferred macrophage mitochondria lack membrane potential yet remain as a distinct population in recipient cancer cells without being degraded or fusing with the host network.
source: These data, taken together with the long-lived observation of the transferred mitochondria in Figure 2a, suggest that transferred macrophage mitochondria lack membrane potential, yet remain as a distinct population in recipient cancer cells, not fusing with the endogenous host mitochondrial network nor subjected to degradation.
evidence: Integration of time-lapse imaging, membrane potential assays, and lysosomal/membrane staining data

claim: Transferred mitochondria are associated with significantly higher levels of oxidized glutathione compared to the host mitochondrial network at 24 and 48 hours.
source: Using a genetically encoded biosensor, mito-Grx1-roGFP2, as a live readout of the mitochondrial glutathione redox state (Gutscher et al., 2008), we found that after 24 and 48 hr, significantly higher ratios of oxidized:reduced protein were associated with the transferred mitochondria versus the host network (Figure 2c–d; Figure 2—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: Ratiometric measurements using mito-Grx1-roGFP2 biosensor in 27 cells (24hr) and 37 cells (48hr) from 3 donors

claim: Transferred mitochondria accumulate higher amounts of reactive oxygen species (ROS).
source: These data indicate that transferred macrophage mitochondria in recipient cells are associated with higher levels of oxidized glutathione, suggesting that they are accumulating higher amounts of ROS.
evidence: Based on mito-Grx1-roGFP2 biosensor measurements showing oxidized glutathione

claim: Transferred mitochondria show more oxidation with the H2O2-specific biosensor mito-roGFP2-Orp1 at 48 hours.
source: Consistent with these results, a second biosensor that is specific for the reactive oxygen species H2O2, mito-roGFP2-Orp1 (Gutscher et al., 2009), also reported more oxidation at the transferred mitochondria compared to the host network (Figure 2—figure supplement 1c–d) after 48 hr of co-culture.
evidence: Ratiometric measurements using mito-roGFP2-Orp1 biosensor in 26 cells from 3 donors at 48hr

claim: ROS accumulate specifically at the site of transferred mitochondria in recipient cancer cells.
source: These results indicate that ROS accumulate at the site of transferred mitochondria in recipient cancer cells.
evidence: Based on two independent biosensor measurements showing localized oxidation at transferred mitochondria

claim: Purified macrophage mitochondria taken up by cancer cells remain distinct and are not encapsulated by membranes after 24 hours.
source: We next determined that purified mitochondria taken up by cancer cells remain distinct, are not encapsulated by membranes after 24 hr (Figure 2—figure supplement 1e), and do not exhibit membrane potential (Figure 2e).
evidence: Microscopy of cancer cells with purified macrophage mitochondria showing lack of MemBrite colocalization and MTDR staining

claim: Cancer cells with internalized purified macrophage mitochondria exhibit increased proliferation in G2/M phase, which is ameliorated by ROS quenching with mitoTEMPO.
source: We found that cancer cells with internalized purified macrophage mitochondria (which, under these conditions, comprise ~1% of the total population) exhibited a significant increase in proliferative cells in the G2/M phase of the cell cycle, compared to sister cells that did not internalize mitochondria (Figure 2f, comparing black bars in lanes 1&2), and that this increase was ameliorated when ROS is quenched with a mitochondrially localized superoxide scavenger, mitoTEMPO (Figure 2f; comparing black bars in lanes 2&4).
evidence: Flow cytometry cell cycle analysis with and without mitoTEMPO treatment (N=3 donors)

claim: ROS quenching does not affect the cell cycle state of cancer cells that did not internalize mitochondria.
source: Importantly, cancer cells that did not internalize mitochondria were not affected by ROS quenching (Figure 2f; comparing black bars in lanes 1&3).
evidence: Flow cytometry showing no change in cell cycle distribution with mitoTEMPO in non-recipient cells

claim: Transferred mitochondria promote proliferation in a ROS-dependent manner.
source: These results indicate that transferred mitochondria promote proliferation in a ROS-dependent manner.
evidence: Based on mitoTEMPO experiments showing ROS scavenging abolishes proliferation increase

claim: Photobleaching mito-KillerRed generates ROS as indicated by increased DCFDA fluorescence.
source: As expected, photobleaching mito-KillerRed+ regions of interest induced ROS (Bass et al., 1983; Figure 2—figure supplement 2a).
evidence: Microscopy showing increased DCFDA signal after photobleaching mito-KillerRed

claim: Cells with induced mitochondrial ROS by photobleaching mito-KillerRed exhibit increased percentage of dividing cells compared to control cells.
source: We found that cells with induced ROS (by photobleaching mito-KillerRed+ regions) exhibited an increased percentage of dividing cells compared to negative control photobleached cells (mito vs. cyto bleach; Figure 2h; Figure 2—figure supplement 2b–c).
evidence: Quantification of cell division over 18 hours in 13 experiments comparing mitochondrial vs cytoplasmic photobleaching

claim: Induction of mitochondrially localized ROS can directly promote cancer cell proliferation.
source: These results indicate that induction of mitochondrially localized ROS can directly promote cancer cell proliferation.
evidence: Based on optogenetic ROS induction experiments showing increased cell division

claim: Cancer cells with macrophage mitochondria have significantly higher cytoplasmic to nuclear ERK-KTR ratios compared to cells without transfer, indicating increased ERK activity.
source: These data show that cancer cells with macrophage mitochondria have significantly higher cytoplasmic to nuclear (C/N) ERK-KTR ratios compared to cells that did not receive mitochondrial transfer, indicating increased ERK activity (Figure 3a–b; Figure 3—figure supplement 2a–b).
evidence: Imaging flow cytometry (Amnis ImageStream) measurements in hundreds of cells from 3 donors

claim: ROS induction by photobleaching mito-KillerRed is sufficient to increase ERK activity in cancer cells.
source: By expressing both mito-KillerRed and ERK-KTR in 231 cells, we induced ROS by photobleaching mito-KillerRed+ regions and found that ROS induction increased ERK-KTR translocation, indicating that ROS induction is sufficient to increase ERK activity in cancer cells (Figure 3c–d; Figure 3—figure supplement 2c).
evidence: Live cell imaging showing ERK-KTR translocation 40 minutes after photobleaching

claim: Treatment with ERK inhibitor (SCH772984 at 1 μM) significantly decreases proliferation of recipient cancer cells with macrophage mitochondria compared to vehicle control.
source: We then found that treatment with ERKi significantly decreased proliferation of recipient 231 cells when compared to vehicle control-treated recipient cells (Figure 3e; Figure 3—figure supplement 4c).
evidence: Flow cytometry cell cycle analysis with ERK inhibitor treatment (N=3 donors)

claim: ERK inhibition specifically decreases proliferation in cancer cells that received macrophage mitochondria, not in cells that did not receive transfer.
source: We further noted that the decrease in proliferation with this concentration of ERK inhibitor was observed only in cancer cells that received macrophage mitochondria, and not in cancer cells that did not receive macrophage mitochondria (bars 2&4 in Figure 3e, compared to bars 1&3), suggesting that the ERK-dependent cell proliferation specifically occurs in cancer cells that received mitochondrial transfer.
evidence: Flow cytometry comparing ERK inhibitor effects in recipient vs non-recipient cells

claim: ERK inhibitor treatment does not alter mitochondrial transfer efficiencies.
source: As a control, we also confirmed that ERKi treatment did not alter mitochondrial transfer efficiencies, showing that ERK signaling does not influence mitochondrial transfer (Figure 3—figure supplement 4d).
evidence: Flow cytometry showing no change in transfer rates with ERK inhibitor (N=3 donors)

claim: Uptake of purified macrophage mitochondria increases the percentage of cancer cells in G2/M phase, which is ameliorated by ERK inhibition.
source: We found that, as before, uptake of purified macrophage mitochondria increased the percentage of cancer cells in the G2/M phase of the cell cycles (Figure 3f, bars 1&2), but that this process is ameliorated by the inhibition of ERK signaling (Figure 3f, bars 2&4).
evidence: Flow cytometry cell cycle analysis with purified mitochondria and ERK inhibitor

claim: ERK inhibition does not affect the cell cycle state of cancer cells that had not taken up purified macrophage mitochondria.
source: We also found that ERK inhibition did not affect the cell cycle state of cancer cells that had not taken up purified macrophage mitochondria (Figure 3f, bars 1&3).
evidence: Flow cytometry showing no effect of ERK inhibitor on non-recipient cells

claim: Mitochondrial transfer promotes cancer cell proliferation through a ROS/ERK-dependent mechanism.
source: Thus, these results indicate that mitochondrial transfer promotes cancer cells proliferation through a ROS/ERK-dependent mechanism.
evidence: Integration of ROS scavenging and ERK inhibition experiments showing both are required for proliferation effect

claim: M2-like macrophages contain significantly more fragmented mitochondria compared to M1-like or M0 macrophages.
source: Activated macrophages were co-cultured with 231 cells, and we first quantified mitochondrial networks using Mitochondrial Network Analyses (MiNA) (Valente et al., 2017). We found that M2-like macrophages contain significantly more fragmented mitochondria when compared to M1-like or M0 (non-activated) macrophages (Figure 4a–b; Figure 4—figure supplement 1a–d).
evidence: Mitochondrial Network Analyses (MiNA) quantification from 2 donors

claim: Mitochondrial transfer efficiencies are significantly increased from M2-like macrophages compared to M1-like or M0 macrophages.
source: We then co-cultured 231 cells with either M0, M1-like, or M2-like macrophages and using flow cytometry, we found that mitochondrial transfer efficiencies were significantly increased from M2-like macrophages when compared to M1-like or non-activated M0 macrophages (Figure 4c).
evidence: Flow cytometry quantification of transfer rates from different macrophage subtypes (N=4 donors)

claim: Macrophages with DRP1 knockdown exhibit hyper-fused mitochondrial networks.
source: To test this hypothesis, we directly manipulated mitochondrial morphology by modulating a key regulator of mitochondrial fission, DRP1 (Fonseca et al., 2019). Macrophages transduced with DRP1-shRNA containing lentivirus exhibited hyper-fused mitochondrial networks (Figure 4d and e) and exhibited decreased mitochondrial transfer (Figure 4f).
evidence: Microscopy and qRT-PCR showing DRP1 knockdown and resulting mitochondrial morphology changes (N=3 donors)

claim: DRP1 knockdown in macrophages decreases mitochondrial transfer to cancer cells.
source: Macrophages transduced with DRP1-shRNA containing lentivirus exhibited hyper-fused mitochondrial networks (Figure 4d and e) and exhibited decreased mitochondrial transfer (Figure 4f).
evidence: Flow cytometry showing reduced transfer rates with DRP1 knockdown (N=3 donors)

claim: Macrophage activation alters mitochondrial dynamics, which directly affects mitochondrial transfer rates.
source: Together these findings reveal that macrophage activation alters mitochondrial dynamics, and that altering mitochondrial dynamics directly affects mitochondrial transfer rates.
evidence: Based on M2 activation and DRP1 knockdown experiments showing correlation between fragmentation and transfer

claim: Transferred mitochondria from M1-like and M2-like macrophages are similarly depolarized as M0 macrophages.
source: Finally, to determine whether the functionality of transferred mitochondria differ between macrophage subtypes, we evaluated the membrane potential of transferred mitochondria, and found that transferred mitochondria from M1-like and M2-like macrophages were similarly depolarized (Figure 4—figure supplement 1e), as to what we observed with M0 macrophages (Figure 2b).
evidence: MTDR and LysoTracker staining showing 100% of transferred mitochondria from M1 and M2 are MTDR-negative

claim: Pro-tumorigenic M2-like macrophages exhibit increased mitochondrial fragmentation, promoting mitochondrial transfer to cancer cells.
source: Taken together, these results suggest that pro-tumorigenic M2-like macrophages exhibit increased mitochondrial fragmentation, promoting mitochondrial transfer to cancer cells.
evidence: Integration of M2 activation, fragmentation analysis, and transfer rate measurements

claim: Mitochondrial transfer occurs from macrophages to patient-derived xenograft organoid (PDxO) cells from both primary breast tumor (HCI-037) and bone metastasis (HCI-038).
source: Mitochondrial transfer was observed from macrophages to both HCI-037 and HCI-038 PDxO cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 2e), although intriguingly, M2-like macrophages preferentially transferred mitochondria to the bone metastasis PDxO cells (HCI-038), whereas M0 and M2-like macrophages transferred mitochondria to primary breast tumor PDxO cells (HCI-037) at the same rate.
evidence: Flow cytometry and live imaging of PDxO co-cultures (N=4 donors)

claim: M2-like macrophages preferentially transfer mitochondria to bone metastasis PDxO cells (HCI-038) compared to primary tumor PDxO cells (HCI-037).
source: Mitochondrial transfer was observed from macrophages to both HCI-037 and HCI-038 PDxO cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 2e), although intriguingly, M2-like macrophages preferentially transferred mitochondria to the bone metastasis PDxO cells (HCI-038), whereas M0 and M2-like macrophages transferred mitochondria to primary breast tumor PDxO cells (HCI-037) at the same rate.
evidence: Flow cytometry showing differential transfer rates between PDxO lines with M2 macrophages

claim: Transferred macrophage mitochondria in PDxO cells lack membrane potential.
source: In all cases, transferred macrophage mitochondria lacked membrane potential (Figure 4—figure supplement 2c), consistent with our results in 231 recipient cells.
evidence: MTDR staining showing transferred mitochondria are MTDR-negative in PDxO cells

claim: In vivo mitochondrial transfer from immune cells to E0771 tumor cells occurs at a rate of 4.8% in bone marrow reconstitution experiments.
source: We found that in vivo mitochondrial transfer occurred at a rate of 4.8%, compared to control transplantation studies at 0.46% (Figure 5a).
evidence: Flow cytometry of tumor cells from mito:mKate2 bone marrow reconstituted mice (N=10 mice per condition)

claim: E0771 tumor cells containing macrophage mitochondria can be observed in vivo using immunohistochemistry in LysM-Cre/MitoTag mice.
source: We injected E0771 cells expressing mito-RFP into these mice with GFP-labeled macrophage mitochondria and observed E0771 cells containing macrophage mitochondria using immunohistochemistry approaches of tumor sections (Figure 5c; Figure 5—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: Immunofluorescence microscopy showing GFP+ mitochondria in mito-RFP+ tumor cells

claim: Recipient tumor cells with macrophage mitochondria exhibit enhanced proliferative capacity compared to tumor cells without transfer in vivo.
source: Using similar cell proliferation analyses as previously described (Figure 1e), we also observed that recipient tumor cells exhibited enhanced proliferative capacity compared to the tumor cells that did not receive transfer (Figure 5d; Figure 5—figure supplement 1c).
evidence: Ki67/DNA flow cytometry analysis of tumor cells from LysM-Cre/MitoTag mice (N=3 mice)

claim: Mammary adenocarcinoma cells with macrophage mitochondria exhibit increased proliferation in vivo.
source: These results show that mammary adenocarcinoma cells with macrophage mitochondria exhibit increased proliferation in vivo.
evidence: Based on in vivo cell cycle analysis showing increased G2/M in recipient tumor cells

claim: With 5% of the cancer cell population receiving mitochondria and a 15% increase in growth rate, an agent-based model predicts a 15% increase in population size after 20 doublings.
source: By 20 divisions, with a 15% increase in growth rate (brown line), even with only 5% of the cancer cell population with macrophage mitochondria at any given time, the model already predicts a 15% increase in population size compared to baseline population rates (comparing the brown line to the blue dotted line).
evidence: Agent-based Monte Carlo simulation modeling population growth with parameters from experimental data

claim: Transferred macrophage mitochondria in cancer cells are dysfunctional and accumulate reactive oxygen species.
source: Collectively, our data explain how a relatively small amount of transferred mitochondria can impact cellular behavior in the recipient cell with fully functioning endogenous mitochondria – Transferred macrophage mitochondria in cancer cells are dysfunctional, ROS accumulates at the site of transferred mitochondria, promoting ERK-mediated cancer cell proliferation.
evidence: Summary statement integrating membrane potential, ROS biosensor, and proliferation data

claim: ROS accumulation at transferred mitochondria promotes ERK-mediated cancer cell proliferation.
source: Collectively, our data explain how a relatively small amount of transferred mitochondria can impact cellular behavior in the recipient cell with fully functioning endogenous mitochondria – Transferred macrophage mitochondria in cancer cells are dysfunctional, ROS accumulates at the site of transferred mitochondria, promoting ERK-mediated cancer cell proliferation.
evidence: Summary statement integrating ROS measurements, ERK activity assays, and proliferation experiments

claim: Cancer cells void of mitochondrial DNA can form tumors by obtaining mitochondria from stromal cells, restoring cancer cell mitochondrial function, cellular respiration, and tumor formation.
source: In animal models, a series of seminal studies revealed that cancer cells void of mitochondrial DNA still form tumors by obtaining mitochondria from stromal cells, thereby restoring cancer cell mitochondrial function, cellular respiration, and tumor formation (Tan et al., 2015; Dong et al., 2017).
evidence: Cited from previous studies by Tan et al., 2015 and Dong et al., 2017

claim: Mitochondrial transfer can alter the metabolic state of recipient cells.
source: Other experiments suggest that mitochondrial transfer not only restores bioenergetics, but can alter the metabolic state of recipient cells (Brestoff et al., 2021; Nicolás-Ávila et al., 2020; Phinney et al., 2015; Saha et al., 2022; Crewe et al., 2021; Korpershoek et al., 2022; Liu et al., 2022; van der Vlist et al., 2022; Yang et al., 2022; Liu et al., 2021), allowing recipient cells to adapt to stressors or changes in the environment, prompting the development of methods targeting mitochondrial dysfunction in disease (Patel et al., 2023; Caicedo et al., 2015).
evidence: Cited from multiple previous studies

claim: Macrophages transfer cytoplasmic contents to cancer cells in vitro and in vivo.
source: We previously reported that macrophages transfer cytoplasmic contents to cancer cells in vitro and in vivo (Roh-Johnson et al., 2017), and hypothesized that a macrophage/cancer cell system would be ideal for probing mitochondrial transfer in cells with functioning mitochondrial networks.
evidence: Cited from previous work by Roh-Johnson et al., 2017

claim: Mitochondria are dynamic organelles known to provide energy for the cell and have a variety of additional essential cellular functions.
source: Mitochondria are dynamic organelles, known to provide energy for the cell, but more recently shown to have a variety of additional essential cellular functions (Zong et al., 2016).
evidence: Cited from Zong et al., 2016 and represents established scientific knowledge

claim: ROS occur normally as byproducts of mitochondrial respiration and can be produced at high levels during organellar dysfunction.
source: One signaling molecule associated with mitochondria is reactive oxygen species (ROS), which occur normally as byproducts of mitochondrial respiration, and can be produced at high levels during organellar dysfunction (Schieber and Chandel, 2014).
evidence: Cited from Schieber and Chandel, 2014 and represents established knowledge

claim: ROS is known to induce several downstream signaling pathways including ERK/MAPK signaling.
source: ROS is known to induce several downstream signaling pathways (Schieber and Chandel, 2014; Brillo et al., 2021), including ERK/MAPK signaling, a pathway known to regulate proliferation and tumorigenesis (Dhillon et al., 2007).
evidence: Cited from multiple sources representing established knowledge

claim: ERK/MAPK signaling is a pathway known to regulate proliferation and tumorigenesis.
source: ROS is known to induce several downstream signaling pathways (Schieber and Chandel, 2014; Brillo et al., 2021), including ERK/MAPK signaling, a pathway known to regulate proliferation and tumorigenesis (Dhillon et al., 2007).
evidence: Cited from Dhillon et al., 2007 representing established knowledge

claim: Macrophage density in solid tumors is associated with disease progression and poor patient prognosis.
source: In many solid tumors, it has long been appreciated that macrophage density is associated with disease progression and poor patient prognosis (Pollard, 2004).
evidence: Cited from Pollard, 2004 representing established knowledge

claim: Macrophages are highly plastic, altering their phenotypes, expression profiles and function depending on environmental stimuli.
source: Macrophages are highly plastic, altering their phenotypes, expression profiles and function, depending on environmental stimuli and conditional requirements (Pan et al., 2020).
evidence: Cited from Pan et al., 2020 representing established knowledge

claim: Macrophages exist in a spectrum of activation states canonically simplified as pro-inflammatory M1-like and anti-inflammatory M2-like macrophages.
source: Accordingly, macrophages exist in a spectrum of activation states but are canonically simplified by the two ends of spectrum: pro-inflammatory and anti-tumorigenic M1-like macrophages; or anti-inflammatory and pro-tumorigenic M2-like macrophages (Huang et al., 2018).
evidence: Cited from Huang et al., 2018 representing established knowledge

claim: Mitochondria with reduced membrane potential can generate ROS.
source: It is possible that ROS are generated by the transferred mitochondria themselves, as previous reports have shown that mitochondria with reduced membrane potential can generate ROS (Feng et al., 2022; Franco-Iborra et al., 2018; Nakai et al., 2003).
evidence: Cited from multiple previous studies

claim: The endoplasmic reticulum can produce ROS in the presence of dysfunctional mitochondria.
source: A previous report showed that the endoplasmic reticulum can produce ROS in the presence of dysfunctional mitochondria (Leadsham et al., 2013), suggesting another possible explanation.
evidence: Cited from Leadsham et al., 2013

claim: Physiological levels of ROS are known second messenger molecules stimulating various pro-survival signaling cascades.
source: Although high levels of ROS are cytotoxic to cells (Stadtman and Levine, 2000; Fruhwirth and Hermetter, 2008; Auten et al., 2002), physiological levels of ROS are known second messenger molecules stimulating various pro-survival signaling cascades (Schieber and Chandel, 2014; Brillo et al., 2021).
evidence: Cited from multiple sources representing established knowledge

claim: A modest increase of mitochondrial-derived ROS can exhibit protective mechanisms through mitohormesis.
source: Additionally, a modest increase of mitochondrial-derived ROS has been shown to exhibit protective mechanisms through mitohormesis (Crewe et al., 2021; Ristow and Schmeisser, 2014), a process in which cellular defense mechanisms are stimulated by sub-lethal stress levels, protecting cells to withstand a secondary exposure.
evidence: Cited from Crewe et al., 2021 and Ristow and Schmeisser, 2014

claim: Mitochondrial transfer has been shown to promote resistance to subsequent chemotherapeutic treatments in healthy neurons and tumor cells.
source: Mitochondrial transfer has been shown to promote resistance to subsequent chemotherapeutic treatments in healthy neurons (English et al., 2020) and tumor cells (Wang et al., 2018; Boukelmoune et al., 2018), however the mechanism of this resistance is unclear.
evidence: Cited from multiple previous studies

claim: Intercellular mitochondrial transport has been implicated in the process of mitochondrial transfer.
source: Although intercellular mitochondrial transport has been implicated in the process of mitochondrial transfer (Boukelmoune et al., 2018; Ahmad et al., 2014), we show that macrophage differentiation directly affects mitochondrial transfer through changes in their mitochondrial morphology.
evidence: Cited from previous studies

claim: Anti-tumor-like (M1-like) macrophages exhibit more glycolytic metabolism, while pro-tumor-like (M2-like) macrophages upregulate oxidative phosphorylation.
source: The relationship between macrophage differentiation and metabolism has been partially defined, with anti-tumor-like (M1-like) macrophages exhibiting more glycolytic metabolism, and pro-tumor-like (M2-like) macrophages upregulating oxidative phosphorylation (Van den Bossche et al., 2017; Mortezaee and Majidpoor, 2022).
evidence: Cited from Van den Bossche et al., 2017 and Mortezaee and Majidpoor, 2022

claim: Mitochondrial fusion supports increases in oxidative phosphorylation in fibroblasts.
source: Studies have indicated that mitochondrial fusion supports increases oxidative phosphorylation in fibroblasts (Yao et al., 2019), however other studies have shown that increasing mitochondrial fission upregulates oxidative phosphorylation in hepatocytes (Zhou et al., 2022).
evidence: Cited from Yao et al., 2019

claim: Increasing mitochondrial fission upregulates oxidative phosphorylation in hepatocytes.
source: Studies have indicated that mitochondrial fusion supports increases oxidative phosphorylation in fibroblasts (Yao et al., 2019), however other studies have shown that increasing mitochondrial fission upregulates oxidative phosphorylation in hepatocytes (Zhou et al., 2022).
evidence: Cited from Zhou et al., 2022

claim: The correlation between mitochondrial morphology and cellular metabolic status is unclear and likely depends on cell type and environmental conditions.
source: Thus, the correlation between mitochondrial morphology and cellular metabolic status is unclear, and these differences are likely due to different cell types and environmental conditions.
evidence: Inference based on conflicting literature about mitochondrial morphology and metabolism

claim: The findings are consistent with several studies describing a metastatic advantage in cancer cells that receive exogenous mitochondria.
source: Our findings are consistent with several studies describing a metastatic advantage in cancer cells that receive exogenous mitochondria (Zampieri et al., 2021; van der Merwe et al., 2021; Dong et al., 2017; Tan et al., 2015).
evidence: Cited from multiple previous studies

claim: Impaired mitophagy and enhanced mitochondrial dysfunction are hallmarks of aging.
source: Impaired mitophagy and enhanced mitochondrial dysfunction are hallmarks of age (Chen et al., 2020), yet little is known about how age-related mitochondrial dysfunction influences mitochondrial transfer.
evidence: Cited from Chen et al., 2020 representing established knowledge

claim: Neurons in an Alzheimer's disease mouse model transfer dysfunctional mitochondria to neighboring astrocytes, contributing to neuronal mitochondrial homeostasis.
source: Interestingly, instead of degrading dysfunctional mitochondria through mitophagy, neurons in an Alzheimer's disease mouse model have been shown to transfer dysfunctional mitochondria to neighboring astrocytes (Lampinen et al., 2022), which contributes to neuronal mitochondrial homeostasis.
evidence: Cited from Lampinen et al., 2022

claim: Age is the greatest known risk factor for Alzheimer's disease.
source: Given that age is the greatest known risk factor of Alzheimer's disease, and most cancers are also age-related, these data collectively warrant broader investigations into how age-associated mitochondrial dysfunction contributes to mitochondrial transfer and how this form of communication may have specific influences on distinct diseased states.
evidence: Represents established medical knowledge

claim: Most cancers are age-related.
source: Given that age is the greatest known risk factor of Alzheimer's disease, and most cancers are also age-related, these data collectively warrant broader investigations into how age-associated mitochondrial dysfunction contributes to mitochondrial transfer and how this form of communication may have specific influences on distinct diseased states.
evidence: Represents established medical knowledge

claim: Mitochondria typically maintain strong membrane potentials, and dysfunctional mitochondria that lack membrane potential are normally degraded or repaired by fusion with healthy mitochondrial networks.
source: The status of transferred mitochondria was unexpected because mitochondria typically maintain strong membrane potentials, and dysfunctional mitochondria that lack membrane potential are normally degraded or repaired by fusion with healthy mitochondrial networks (Phinney et al., 2015).
evidence: Cited from Phinney et al., 2015 and represents established knowledge about mitochondrial quality control

claim: MDA-MB-231 cells are capable of performing mitophagy.
source: This model raises several fascinating questions, including when and how transferred mitochondria become depolarized and accumulate ROS, where the ROS is generated in the recipient cell, and why depolarized mitochondria are not repaired or degraded in the recipient cell, given that 231 cells are capable of performing mitophagy (Biel and Rao, 2018).
evidence: Cited from Biel and Rao, 2018

claim: Lateral mitochondrial transfer can affect cellular and tissue homeostasis.
source: Recent studies reveal that lateral mitochondrial transfer, the movement of mitochondria from one cell to another, can affect cellular and tissue homeostasis.
evidence: Summary of recent literature representing current understanding in the field

claim: The paradigm in the field is that functional transferred mitochondria restore bioenergetics and revitalize cellular functions to recipient cells with damaged or non-functional mitochondrial networks.
source: Most of what we know about mitochondrial transfer stems from bulk cell studies and have led to the paradigm that functional transferred mitochondria restore bioenergetics and revitalize cellular functions to recipient cells with damaged or non-functional mitochondrial networks.
evidence: Summary of prevailing paradigm in the field based on previous literature

claim: Mitochondrial transfer also occurs between cells with functioning endogenous mitochondrial networks.
source: However, we show that mitochondrial transfer also occurs between cells with functioning endogenous mitochondrial networks, but the mechanisms underlying how transferred mitochondria can promote such sustained behavioral reprogramming remain unclear.
evidence: Based on the experimental system used in this study with MDA-MB-231 cells

claim: Transferred macrophage mitochondria activate downstream signaling pathways in a ROS-dependent manner in cancer cells.
source: Collectively these results indicate that transferred macrophage mitochondria activate downstream signaling pathways in a ROS-dependent manner in cancer cells, and provide a model of how sustained behavioral reprogramming can be mediated by a relatively small amount of transferred mitochondria in vitro and in vivo.
evidence: Summary conclusion integrating all experimental findings

claim: Macrophage mitochondrial transfer promotes tumor cell proliferation in vivo.
source: Finally, we observe that macrophage mitochondrial transfer promotes tumor cell proliferation in vivo.
evidence: Based on in vivo experiments in two mouse models showing increased proliferation in recipient tumor cells

source: Collectively these results indicate that transferred macrophage mitochondria activate downstream signaling pathways in a ROS-dependent manner in cancer cells, and provide a model of how sustained behavioral reprogramming can be mediated by a relatively small amount of transferred mitochondria in vitro and in vivo.
